Recall that the equation of a hyperboloid of one sheet centered at $O$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1,
$$

and a hyperboloid of one sheet centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}-\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=1,
$$

Thus, our equation is a hyperboloid of one sheet with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(-1,3,1),\,a=b=c=1.
$$

Recall that the equation of a hyperboloid of two sheets centered at $O$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=-1,
$$

and a hyperboloid of two sheets centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}-\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}=-1,
$$

Thus, our equation is a hyperboloid of two sheets with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(-1,0,2),\,a=\sqrt{3},\,b=2,\,c=1.
$$

Recall that the equation of a parabolic cylinder, whose axis is the $z$-axis, is given by

$$
{x}^{2}=4py.
$$

Thus, our equation is a parabolic cylinder with $p=2.$

Recall that the equation of a hyperbolic cylinder, whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis, is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1,
$$

and a hyperbolic cylinder, whose axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ in the $xy$-plane, is given by

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Thus, our equation is a hyperbolic cylinder with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(-2,1),\,a=b=1.
$$

Recall that the equation of a parabolic cylinder, whose axis is the $z$-axis, is given by

$$
{x}^{2}=4py,
$$

and a parabolic cylinder, shifted ${x}_{0}$ along the x-axis and ${y}_{0}$ along the y-axis, is given by

$$
(x-{x}_{0})^{2}=4p(y-{y}_{0}).
$$

Thus, our equation is a parabolic cylinder with the following parameters:

$$
({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(-2,0),\,p=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square in the $y$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}+8y+9{z}^{2}-5x+9 & =0 \\ 4({y}^{2}+2y)+9{z}^{2}-5x+9 & =0 \\ 4[(y+1)^{2}-1]+9{z}^{2}-5x+9 & =0 \\ 4(y+1)^{2}-4+9{z}^{2}-5x+9 & =0 \\ 4(y+1)^{2}+9{z}^{2}-5x+5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}4(y+1)^{2}+9{z}^{2}-5x+5 & =0 \\ 4(y+1)^{2}+9{z}^{2} & =5(x-1) \\ \frac{4(y+1)^{2}}{5}+\frac{9{z}^{2}}{5} & =x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of an elliptic paraboloid centered at $(1,-1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+12y-z+13 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3({y}^{2}+4y)-z+13 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3[(y+2)^{2}-4]-z+13 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3(y+2)^{2}-12-z+13 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3(y+2)^{2}-z+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3(y+2)^{2}-z+1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3(y+2)^{2} & =z-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of an elliptic paraboloid centered at $(0,-2,1).$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square in the $x$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+2x+y & =0 \\ -({x}^{2}-2x)+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by rearranging, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}-(x-1)^{2}+1+{z}^{2}+y & =0 \\ -(x-1)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-y-1 \\ (x-1)^{2}-{z}^{2} & =y+1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid centered at $(1, -1, 0).$
